items.title: Ramayana Part 1: Having courted propaganda, Bollywood finds itself held hostage by it
items.summary: In one of the scenes in Nitesh Tiwari’s Ramayana: Part 1 , Ram (Ranbir Kapoor) asks what the purpose of his birth is. He is vulnerable, confused, and deeply shaken by the odds that have consecutively been stacked against him. It is only in those fleeting moments, towards the end of the film, that we get some insight into the protagonist’s conflict in an adaptation that is otherwise deliberately held back. And this denial of interiority is neither without purpose nor limited to Ram. Nitesh’s cinematic iteration of Valmiki’s epic anchors itself on caution. Everything is calculated, tepid even, in what seems like an attempt to prevent the story from making any detour that may offend bhakts or stir up controversy. But in its anxiety to avoid transgression, the film also relinquishes the artistic freedom to complicate inherited truths. By doing so, it reveals itself as a propaganda machine which flattens the interpretative potential of art and instead makes it a vehicle for cultural consolidation. The irony, then, is hard to miss. In trying meticulously to offend no one, Nitesh Tiwari’s Ramayana: Part 1 appears to have not pleased people either. For viewers who lean towards a more liber

items.title: Could you survive without Microsoft? Inside the costs of digital dependence
items.summary: When I arrived at work to discover that Outlook had vanished from my computer, I wondered how I was supposed to get through my working day. No emails. No calendar. No meeting invitations. Then another thought crossed my mind: when did we become so dependent on a single technology company that losing access to one application could disrupt our entire working routine? And what is the financial and environmental cost of that dependence? We regularly discuss sustainability in terms of reducing plastic, cutting carbon emissions and consuming less energy. But the digital systems we rely on every day also have huge environmental consequences. As world leaders gather at the UN climate summit, Cop31 , in Turkey, perhaps it is time to ask an uncomfortable question: can our digital economy really become sustainable when so much of it depends on a handful of technology companies? The cloud has a physical footprint The cloud may sound weightless, but it runs on data centres, electricity, cooling systems and hardware. items.title: Microsoft has suffered a global outage. A tech expert explains what went wrong
items.summary: Microsoft has suffered a major global outage, bringing many of its widely used tools, including email and cloud storage, to a standstill. According to outage tracking site DownDetector, some 130,000 people reported issues accessing Microsoft Outlook as of early Thursday afternoon US Eastern time (early Friday morning in Sydney). In a statement on X , the tech giant said it was “aggressively pursuing all pathways to reduce impact” and “restarting affected servers to return them to service”. In an article for The Conversation last month, I explained how the whole internet is unlikely to go down but several services can become unavailable together when they rely on shared systems. This outage shows precisely what happens when that shared infrastructure fails – and why we must prepare for digital outages in a similar way we do for natural disasters. items.title: Keralam: Muslims step in to help with two Hindu women's final rites
items.summary: Since childhood, Kalyani Amma has been simply "Amma" to Razak, now a 51-year-old. "She is not 'like my mother'; she is my mother," he says. It's a feeling shared by his younger brother Sulaiman. On November 7, when the 86-year-old died in Vaduvanchal, Wayanad, she had no children or living relatives. Razak and Sulaiman performed her last rites according to Hindu rites. Some 115 km away in Pallikkara, Malappuram, the Khadeeja mosque opened its doors for the last rites of another Hindu woman on November 10. Premalatha, 52, lived in a rented house too small for her body to be bathed and prepared for the final rites. The mosque offered its grounds instead. Both the incidents became headlines but it wasn't anything unusual for the people who were involved in it. For them, living together peacefully and offering support to neighbors is simply a normal way of life, rather than an extraordinary deed deserving public attention. ‘She is my mother’ Kalyani Amma worked multiple jobs to make a living; she had a cattle and used to do cleaning work at a private bank.
